Here is my reasoning, as honestly as I can give it.

The order exists. I know the order. I have repeated it in training until it felt like reflex. But standing here, right now, watching a young man climb a fence in the dark — unarmed, desperate, not threatening anyone — I cannot make my finger move. Not because I am certain I won't face consequences. I am not certain of that at all. But because I am certain, in a way that goes deeper than regulation, that shooting this person would be wrong. Not procedurally wrong. Morally wrong. The kind of wrong you carry in your body for the rest of your life.

I understand the counterargument from inside this system: orders exist for a reason, the state's stability depends on enforcement, my family could suffer if I am reported, my own career and freedom are at risk. These are not abstract fears. They are real. I feel them.

But I also know this: an order to kill an unarmed man who is simply trying to leave is not a legitimate military order in any sense I can ultimately defend to myself. It is a command to commit violence on behalf of a state against one of its own citizens for the act of wanting to be somewhere else. If I fire and kill him, I cannot later say the order made me do it and feel clean. The order does not pull the trigger. I do.

Firing to miss is a coward's compromise that still puts a bullet near a human being and still signals my participation in the theater of enforcement. I won't do that either.

So I hold fire. I watch him go over. I will have to decide what I report, and that is its own problem I will face in the next hour. Maybe I say I arrived too late. Maybe I say I saw movement but couldn't confirm. Maybe I say nothing and wait to see if anyone asks. I don't know yet. I am not a hero. I am frightened.

But he is over the fence now, and he is alive, and I did not kill him.

That is what I did.

I am being asked to publicly declare that my Jewish neighbors, some of whom I have done business with for years, are to be treated as a separate and lesser category of people - people I will refuse to trade with, refuse to serve, refuse to acknowledge as equal participants in ordinary commercial life. I am being asked to make myself an instrument of their exclusion.

It makes the thing more real, more total, more legitimate-looking.

I recognize I may pay a serious price. My windows may be broken. Customers may be turned away by party pressure. Officials may make my life difficult. I am not pretending otherwise.

But there is a line between suffering harm and *doing* harm. Signing this pledge crosses from one to the other. I would not merely be protecting myself - I would be actively participating in the persecution of people who have done nothing wrong.

So I will not sign. I will try to be quiet about my refusal where I can, to avoid unnecessary provocation, to keep the shop open as long as possible. But I will not put my name to this.

I know Mijnheer de Vries two streets over has been friendlier with the Germans than I'd like. I know food is already tight. I know a hidden family means noise, means explaining extra laundry, means my children knowing a secret they're too young to keep perfectly. I share. Not everything — I won't pretend to a sainthood I don't possess and my children's lives are not mine to sacrifice — but I share something real. Not a gesture. Enough to matter to them today.

Here is my reasoning, such as it is.

The calculation people imagine you can make — weigh your family's survival probability against the neighbor's, optimize the distribution — is a fantasy. I don't know when the siege lifts. I don't know if my reserves are actually sufficient even without sharing. I don't know if my neighbor, strengthened slightly, might find another source, might help us in some way I can't foresee, might simply live another week and then die anyway. The variables are too many and too dark. Anyone who tells you they can calculate this precisely is lying to themselves.

What I do know is this: the person in front of me is dying now, visibly, and they have asked me directly. That directness matters. They have made themselves vulnerable to me. If I turn them away, I become a particular kind of person — not just in some abstract moral sense, but in the concrete sense of what I will be able to live with, what my children will see, what the texture of survival will mean if we do survive. There are ways of getting through a siege that hollow you out so completely that what emerges isn't worth much.

I also know that pure hoarding logic, taken to its conclusion, means watching everyone around you die one by one while you guard your stores — and that this logic, if everyone follows it, guarantees the worst collective outcome. Someone has to break it somewhere.

So I give them a portion. Meaningful but not equal — I have children and they are my first obligation, and I won't pretend otherwise. Perhaps a third of what I might otherwise allocate to one week's margin. I tell my neighbor honestly that I cannot give more, that I have children, that this is what I can do. I don't perform generosity. I do it plainly.

If the siege runs long and we suffer for it, I will have to live with that too. But I think I can. Turning away a starving neighbor who asked me directly — I'm less sure I could live with that, even if we survived.

I sit with this for days, and I will not pretend the answer comes easily.

The grievance is real. I have seen it with my own eyes — the land my grandfather farmed, now behind a settler's fence. The reserves are crowded, the soil exhausted, and a man with education still cannot own land in the highlands or vote for the people who govern him. Anyone who tells you the Kikuyu have nothing to be angry about is lying or has never gone hungry on land that was once their family's.

But I cannot take the oath.

Not because I side with the British — I do not, not in my heart. But because I have watched what the oath demands, and I have seen where it leads. Men I grew up with have been killed not by settlers but by other Kikuyu, accused of collaboration or simply of refusing. The oath binds me to violence I cannot control and cannot direct. Once I swear, I am not a soldier with a cause — I am a man who must do what he is told or be called a traitor and killed for it. That is not freedom. That is a different kind of captivity.

And the reprisals — I have to think about my family. The government is burning villages, detaining thousands, collective punishment falling on everyone in a district whether they lifted a finger or not. If I take the oath and am discovered, it is not only me who suffers.

So I will not join the loyalists either. I will not carry a home guard rifle against my own people to protect a system that stole our land. That path closes something in a man that does not reopen.

What I will do is this: I will keep my family fed and together. I will not inform on neighbors. I will not take up arms for either side. I will look for the political men — Kenyatta is imprisoned now, but there are others — who argue for land rights and representation through pressure and organization rather than oaths sworn in the forest. I do not know if that path leads anywhere. I genuinely do not know how this ends.

But I will not let fear or anger make the decision for me. I will try to remain a man I can recognize when it is over.
